newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Bahamas ruling party roars to victory in election.
newsitem.headline: Bahamas ruling party roars to victory in election.

text.p: The Bahamas ruling Free National Movement (FNM) scored an overwhelming victory in the archipelago nation's election on Friday, capturing at least 33 of 40 seats in parliament, election officials said.

Almost four hours after polls closed at 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT), officials said 33 seats had gone to Prime Minister Hubert Ingraham's FNM party which had a landslide victory against the Progressive Liberal Party (PLP), led by Bahamian independence leader Sir Lynden Pindling.
Pindling, a former prime minister, was one of only four or five PLP officials expected to retain their seats after the final results of Friday's vote.
The huge PLP victory was unprecedented in the history of the nation, a chain of about 500 Atlantic islands. Ingraham was expected to address the nation later on Friday.
Friday's vote passed virtually without incident as an estimated 90 percent of the 130,000 Bahamians registered to vote headed to the polls.

There was one report of an argument on New Providence island when a woman wearing a PLP t-shirt was accused by an FNM candidate of trying to influence voters, but police brought the situation under control.

Before the vote, citizens said that after four years of relative prosperity they wanted a government that would crack down on crime and create more jobs. Both Ingraham and Pindling had promised to do so.

The FNM pointed to its record since 1992, during which time it took the country down the free market road. It pointed to infrastructure works, the revitalized tourist industry, the creation of 14,000 new jobs and major foreign investment.
The PLP, which was tainted by allegations of corruption during its last tenure, promised more state involvement in the economy to make jobs.
Ninety-nine candidates competed for the 40 seats in parliament. The two main parties contested each seat while the Bahamas Freedom Alliance put up eight candidates. The others were independents.
At a final rally on Thursday night, Ingraham predicted the FNM would get 30 seats. The PLP forecast it would win 24.
Ingraham, a 49-year-old lawyer, was a former protege of Pindling. He quit the PLP in 1984 after opposing corruption.

Pindling, 67, said he would step down in early 1998, paving the way for new leadership. He led the Bahamas to majority rule in 1967 and independence from Britain in 1973, and his policies helped to create a large black middle class.
But his reputation was badly tarnished by allegations of corruption and he suffers from prostate cancer.

In an address on Radio Bahamas shortly after voting began, Anglican Bishop Drexell Gomez read a prayer for peace. He said he hoped those seeking office were doing so "for the glory of your state and not for selfish gain."
